Jabbok
JAB-uhk
proper noun (place)
Hebrew Yabboq, a river east of the Jordan; the ford where Jacob wrestled with God and was renamed Israel.

See also: Jabbok

Biblical Definition

The Jabbok was a river flowing west into the Jordan from the highlands of Gilead, most famous as the scene of Jacob's night of wrestling with God. Returning to meet his brother Esau in great fear, Jacob sent his family and goods across the ford of Jabbok and was left alone; "and there wrestled a man with him until the breaking of the day" (Gen 32:24). The Man — the Angel of the LORD, God Himself in visible form — touched the hollow of Jacob's thigh, so that he limped ever after, yet Jacob clung to Him crying, "I will not let thee go, except thou bless me" (Gen 32:26). There God changed his name from Jacob ("supplanter") to Israel, "for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed." Jacob named the place Peniel, "for I have seen God face to face, and my life is preserved" (Gen 32:30). The Jabbok was also later a boundary of the Ammonites and of the trans-Jordan tribes. It stands in the dictionary as the river of Jacob's transformation, where the supplanter became Israel, where prevailing prayer clung to God and would not let go, and where the man who wrestled God came away both broken and blessed, limping yet a prince.

Webster 1828 Definition

A river east of the Jordan (Gen 32:22-30) where Jacob wrestled with God all night, was renamed Israel, and named the place Peniel ("I have seen God face to face"); the river of transformation and prevailing prayer.

JABBOK, proper noun. A river east of the Jordan, flowing from Gilead.

Where Jacob sent his family across and was left alone (Gen 32:22-24).

Where he wrestled with God (the Angel of the LORD) till daybreak.

Where his name was changed from Jacob to Israel.

Where he named the place Peniel: "I have seen God face to face" (Gen 32:30).

Key Scripture

Gen 32:24 — "And Jacob was left alone; and there wrestled a man with him until the breaking of the day."

Gen 32:26 — "And he said, Let me go, for the day breaketh. And he said, I will not let thee go, except thou bless me."

Gen 32:28 — "And he said, Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel: for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed."

Hos 12:4 — "Yea, he had power over the angel, and prevailed: he wept, and made supplication unto him: he found him in Bethel, and there he spake with us;"

Modern Corruption

Jabbok needs no defense from redefinition; its lesson is the transforming encounter with God in prevailing prayer, where the believer is both broken and blessed, made to limp and made a prince.

expand to see more

Self-sufficiency correction. Jacob the supplanter had schemed and grasped his whole life; at the Jabbok God broke his self-reliance, touching his thigh so he limped ever after. The dictionary holds that God often must wound our self-sufficiency before He can bless us; the prince Israel was made not by Jacob's cunning but by his clinging, and the man who would have power with God must first be broken of his power in himself.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is prevailing prayer that will not let go. Jacob clung to God crying, "I will not let thee go, except thou bless me" (Gen 32:26); Hosea says "he wept, and made supplication unto him" (Hos 12:4). The dictionary commends this holy importunity: the believer is invited to wrestle with God in prayer, to cling to His promises, and to refuse to release his hold until the blessing comes — coming away, like Jacob, both humbled and crowned.
